name: United Kingdom
summary_text: The national equality body code on single-sex spaces came into force in August 2026. It requires enforcement on the basis of biological sex and gives organisations practical examples for compliance in toilets, changing rooms and similar spaces.  On 19 June 2026 Judge Lady Ross in the Outer House of the Court of Session, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, struck down the Scottish Prison Service non-statutory guidance on custody of trans prisoners as unlawful. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching gender identity rather than sex at birth. The court held that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis, addressing Equality Act 2010 Sch.22(1), the Prison Rules, the Gender Recognition Act 2004 and Article 8.  Litigation around the Scottish prison guidance included competing claims heard by the Court of Session. Counsel argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk. For Women Scotland challenged the guidance to require only biological females in the women’s estate, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible.  British Transport Police adopted an interim position after the Supreme Court ruling on sex. Trans women are to be strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth. The prior policy had permitted trans women staff holding a Gender Recognition Certificate to intimately search women.  Police Scotland published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 for searching transgender persons. Searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex in custody and stop-and-search. Where lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of the individual’s lived gender on request.  In December 2023 the United Kingdom government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and United States states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium. The stated reason was that those jurisdictions allowed transition too easily. People from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change legal gender in the United Kingdom.  Legal gender recognition has been available under the Gender Recognition Act 2004, effective 4 April 2005. The Act followed Goodwin v United Kingdom (2002), where the United Kingdom was found in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights after Corbett v Corbett (1970) had prevented change of the sex marker on birth certificates. Since 2005 a transgender person may apply to the Gender Recognition Panel after two years transitioned, without mandatory sex reassignment surgery, to obtain a new birth certificate and full legal recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. A married applicant was originally required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance, with re-registration only through dissolution and later civil partnership. Under current law a certificate will not be issued unless the spouse consents, and the marriage must be terminated if consent is refused.  TransActual UK’s Gendered Spaces Report 2025 surveyed trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents. The results corroborated fears of harassment from those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces. The full report was published as a PDF.  On 18 August 2026 United Nations human rights experts warned that United Kingdom revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.  Northern Ireland operates under different equality legislation. Authorities there were still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling on sex at the time of the August 2026 reporting.  Same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales under the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013, in force 13 March 2014, in Scotland in 2014, and in Northern Ireland on 13 January 2020 after United Kingdom Parliament intervention. Civil partnerships have been available since 2005 and give most but not all rights of marriage, with recognition problems in some other countries.
